newsitem.title: USA: Few policyholders oppose Prudential settlement.
newsitem.headline: Few policyholders oppose Prudential settlement.

text.p: Prudential Insurance Co of America said only a very few policyholders have opposed its proposed class-action settlement of sales abuse allegations.

In a court document outlining its defense of the settlement, Prudential said only 0.26 percent, or about one-eighth of one percent of the class members, owning about 10.7 million policies, have chosen to opt out the settlement.
An even smaller number, about 300, have raised objections to the terms of the settlement, according to the documents.
Under the settlement, Prudential has agreed to pay at least $410 million and additional compensation as well.
Prudential said it also has agreed to a blanket waiver of statute of limitations and other defenses, which could have posed significant bars to recovery by many class members.
Opponents and supporters of the proposed settlement will have a chance to present their arguments at a hearing scheduled for February 24 before U.S. district judge Alfred Wolin in Newark, N.J.

Some of the biggest opposition to the proposed settlement has come from four states, which claim the deal places to much of a burden on customers to prove that fraudulent misrepresentations were made when the bought their policies.

These states, Florida, Massachusetts, Texas and California, want all policyholders, before entering the proposed dispute resolution process, to be assured of receiving significant relief merely by claiming to have been misled, unless Prudential can prove otherwise, Prudential said in the document.
Prudential said such a provision would not only destroy the proposed settlement and dispute resolution process, "but would be egregiously unfair to Prudential and all of its mutual policyholders."

Prudential said such a provision would "create a stampede of claims by those who know only that they are guaranteed payment" because they bought the disputed policies "from the right company at the right time."
Policyholders who bought permanent life insurance from 1982 to 1995 may be eligible for relief under the settlement.

Prudential said such a provision would overcompensate some policyholders and diminish its surplus, resulting in lower dividend payments to the vast majority of Prudential policyholders, who do not feel misled and do not seek to assert any claims.
Some policyholders claim they were improperly pressured into buying new life insurance policies, using the cash value of their existing policies to finance them.
Prudential argued that the use of policy cash values or accumulated dividends to finance the purchase of new insurance is neither improper nor illegal.
"Only misleading and deceptive sales practices -- which the ADR plan is structured to address -- have been outlawed," Prudential said.
Prudential also defended the dispute resolution process against claims it is too complicated and burdensome.
Instead, Prudential said many of the objections are in error and do not reflect how the process actually works.
Prudential also said that document destruction will not adversely affect claims.
Prudential earlier this year was fined $1 million for its role in destroying documents relevant to the class-action case.
Prudential said it recently agreed to add to the plan specific enhanced provisions for scoring claims for incidents of document destruction.
In addition, Prudential said it is taking steps in cooperation with the lead counsel, regulators and court to identify and remedy past destruction and prevent future destruction of documents.
-- Patricia Vowinkel 212-859-1716
